rejected.title: Statistical claims
card: A statistical claim is only as good as the data behind it. Ask who collected the data, how they collected it and how many people or items it covers.

Check who is in the sample. If it leaves out part of the group the claim is about, or only includes people who chose to reply, the result may be biased. A very small sample can also give a result that does not hold for the whole group.

Look for errors and misleading uses. If a graph's vertical axis does not start at zero, each bar shows only the part above the starting value, so a small gap can look huge. A percentage with no sample size, or a claim that one thing caused another when the data only shows they happen together, is also misleading.
For example, a gym says 90% of members love its classes, but it asked only 10 members, all leaving a class. The sample is small and the people were not chosen fairly, so the claim is weak.
rejected.remember: Before trusting a claim, check the sample, the numbers and how the graph is drawn.

a.q: A shop claims 80% of customers prefer its brand. It asked 5 people standing at its own checkout. What is the main problem?
opts: Only 5 people, all at its own checkout, were asked
80% of 5 people is not a whole number of people
A result as high as 80% is too high to be believed
The result needs to be shown on a graph to count
a.why: Five people who are already buying at the checkout is a tiny sample that is likely to favour the brand. The arithmetic is fine, since 80% of 5 is 4 people, so the problem is who was asked and how many.
a.clue: Think about how many people were asked and who they were.

b.q: A graph shows a town's bike sales rising from 520 to 540, yet the second bar looks twice as tall as the first. What is the most likely cause?
opts: The vertical axis starts at 500, not at zero
Sales doubled, so the bars are drawn correctly
The axis starts at zero but uses steps of 20
Bars always exaggerate change compared with lines
b.why: Measured from 500, the bars are 20 and 40 units tall, so the second looks twice as tall. Sales did not double: 540 is only about 4% more than 520. An axis from zero would make the bars almost the same height.
b.clue: Bar height shows the distance above the axis's starting value.

a.q: A shop claims 80% of customers prefer its brand. It asked 5 people standing at its own checkout. What is the main problem?
opts: The sample is tiny and taken only from its own customers
The percentage was worked out by dividing wrongly
The shop should have asked more than one question
The result is too high to be believed
a.why: Five people from the shop's own checkout is a very small sample and is likely to favour the brand. The percentage itself may be correct, so the problem is the data, not the arithmetic.
a.clue: Look at how many people were asked and where.

b.q: A graph shows a town's bike sales rising from 520 to 540. Its vertical axis starts at 500, so the second bar looks twice as tall. What is misleading?
opts: The axis does not start at zero, so a small rise looks large
The sales rose, so the graph should not be used
The graph uses bars rather than a line
The numbers 520 and 540 are too close together
b.why: Starting the axis at 500 cuts off most of each bar, so a rise of 20 looks huge. Rising sales are not misleading, and the type of graph is not the problem.
b.clue: Check where the vertical axis begins.
